name: Esther Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. What does a normal day bring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Esther Larsen, 43, and I'm still a junior worker on residential building sites. I left school early, and I am learning basic carpentry later than most people in the crew. I fix backing blocks, carry boards and help square up door openings; the lead checks my cuts. I enjoy making a house safe for a family, but I hate being moved along before someone explains why a door binds.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, what depends on your pay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Pavel does seasonal grounds work, and our children are eight and thirteen. We have a mortgage and around five months of expenses saved, mostly for the winter when his hours fall. I earn ordinary site pay; there are some other building firms nearby, but I would need a recommendation to get in. I don't use AI tools. I carry the drawing in a plastic sleeve and ask the lead when a line is unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that if an office machine saves a form, fine, but it must still send the right door and hinges. I would not want a screen to replace the lead checking a frame before we hang it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work ought to carry on, but a slow building month at the same time as Pavel's winter gap would eat our reserve. Five months saved sounds like plenty until both wages pause and the mortgage takes its share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to the same sites and ask the lead to let me practise hanging one door from start to finish on a paid shift. In the first year I'd keep my paper checks and, if a new ordering form appeared, have the storekeeper explain it to me before I signed anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. AI does little in this picture, yet two seasonal wages and a mortgage can make an ordinary quiet month heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a full door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep getting the middle jobs, like carrying the hinges, and then I don't see why a door scrapes. One complete door would teach me more than six errands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you handle the winter gap now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We leave the savings for the mortgage and heating, and my sister helps with school pickups when Pavel gets a short job far away. I want us to carry our own bills as far as we can.

say: I would accept small **office shortcuts** if the correct door and hinges arrive.
I would keep the lead’s **frame check** before hanging a door.
think: My **site wage** should continue under mild AI change.
A site slowdown plus Pavel’s **winter gap** could drain savings.
do: Keep **paid site shifts** and practise hanging one full door.
Use **paper checks** and request an explanation of any new order form.
feel: **Uneasy** about seasonal wages and mortgage payments.
S0.quote: Five months saved sounds like plenty until both wages pause and the mortgage takes its share.
fieldNote: Esther expects little AI effect on **hands-on tasks**, while two seasonal earnings keep her from feeling financially secure.
She wants **complete paid practice** on a door and uses family help for pickups without treating it as income.

steps.text: Keep paid site shifts on current residential projects
Ask lead for paid start-to-finish door-hanging practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the builder to show the crew what a faster schedule means for the number of paid days, not just for completion dates. A neat plan cannot square a door opening in an old house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the office to use AI for orders and planning, then try to fit the same work into a shorter site rota. I'm a junior hand and could be sent home first; Pavel's grounds work would not cover our mortgage if my days fell for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current shifts and ask the lead for more paid time on door repairs. During the first year I'd compare the new rota with my pay slips, ask the manager directly why days were cut, and apply to the two renovation builders my cousin knows if the reduction lasts a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can work hard, but I cannot make a missing Friday wage appear by praising a new schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask your cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Leena delivers paint to those builders and knows when they have real jobs, not just a sign outside. I would ask for an introduction, then speak for myself about what I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the planning software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the boss makes it part of my work and shows me what to press. I do not learn a whole new system by poking at it after a shift.

say: I would ask how a faster schedule changes **paid days**.
I would remind managers that old door openings still need **hands-on fitting**.
think: My **junior rota** could shrink after faster office planning.
Pavel’s seasonal **grounds wage** cannot replace mine for months.
do: Keep **current shifts** and request paid door-repair practice.
Check **pay slips** against the new rota and ask about cuts.
Apply to **two renovation builders** after a month of lower hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a sustained fall in site pay.
S1.quote: I cannot make a missing Friday wage appear by praising a new schedule.
fieldNote: She judges the new schedule by **pay slips**, not a forecast, because a junior worker is easy to send home.
Her **cousin’s introduction** is a realistic route to local openings, while she still must demonstrate her developing skill.

steps.text: Keep working current paid residential site shifts
Ask lead for paid door-repair practice
Apply to two renovation builders if reduced hours last a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Pavel that AGI might take the drawings and buying by 2028, but hands-on robots arrive about 2031. I would still go to site while there is work, and I would ask our family what help is possible if the wage stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work is mostly in the office, yet the builder could still cut helpers once plans get cheaper. By 2031 robots able to hang doors and carry boards could replace my junior hours completely. Five months of savings will not raise two children or pay a mortgage through a long job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask a local repair firm whether it offers paid apprenticeships to older starters and apply if the answer is yes. In 2029 I'd keep taking safe site shifts; if my hours fell, Pavel and I would call the mortgage lender, and I would ask my sister about temporary school pickups while I looked for paid repair work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have learned enough to know how much I still don't know, and a machine that works faster with its hands leaves me little time to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could your sister do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Ana could pick up the eight-year-old after school if I had to travel to a paid repair placement. She cannot pay our mortgage, and I would not ask her to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are repairs safer after robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot promise that. A robot that can hang a door could learn to repair one too; I would take the apprenticeship for wages and experience now, not a guarantee forever.

say: I would explain **2028 AGI** before **2031 robots** to Pavel.
I would ask family for **childcare help** if I need to travel for paid work.
think: My **helper hours** could fall even before physical robots arrive.
I expect my **junior site wage** to vanish once robots do fitting.
do: Apply for a **paid adult apprenticeship** if a repair firm offers one.
Contact the **lender** and ask Ana for pickups if hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss beyond the savings bridge.
S2.quote: Five months of savings will not raise two children or pay a mortgage through a long job search.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **2028 planning** from 2031 physical automation while anticipating that helpers may be cut at both stages.
Her family can provide **school pickups**, not money; she looks for paid apprenticeship rather than imagining unpaid study is affordable.

steps.text: Apply for paid adult repair apprenticeship if local firm offers one
Keep taking safe residential site shifts in 2029
Call mortgage lender and ask sister Ana for pickups if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives us time to teach people properly on the job, if builders still want to train junior hands. AGI changes drawings in 2031, and robots reach the door frames around 2034; we need paid work through both dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might still be on site while AGI writes the orders, though the crew could be smaller. At 51 in 2034 robots may hang doors without me; I expect fewer paid days, but a longer warning could let me become a reliable repair worker first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lead this year for one paid repair shift a fortnight and keep a notebook of doors that close properly after I fix them. By 2032 I'd ask a renovation firm to look at that record and apply for a paid place; in the first year after 2031 I'd keep working from checked paper drawings while asking which site hours remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It would help to have time for mistakes and correction while wages still come in, though I cannot make a firm hire me by keeping a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a good repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A door that closes without rubbing after the lead checks the frame and the hinges. I would ask the owner to sign off only after they have used it, not because I want the job crossed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the crew before a repair offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need the regular site wage and Pavel's winter work is uncertain. A written offer with paid hours would change my mind.

say: I would ask builders for **paid on-site teaching** before robots reach door work.
I would separate **2031 drawings** from **2034 fitting**.
think: My **site days** may thin after AGI changes orders.
A **repair record** might help me compete for paid work before 2034.
do: Take **paid repair shifts** fortnightly if the lead agrees.
Show **finished-door records** to a renovation firm by 2032.
Keep **site wages** and use checked paper drawings after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to correct mistakes before wage pressure grows.
S3.quote: A written offer with paid hours would change my mind.
fieldNote: Esther would risk changing builders for a **written paid offer**, while refusing to leave current wages for an uncertain promise.
Her **door-repair notebook** is evidence of supervised practice, not an assumption of safety after physical robots arrive.

steps.text: Ask lead for one paid repair shift every fortnight
Apply to renovation firm by 2032 with finished-door record
Keep paid residential site shifts after AGI arrives in 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn useful work and stay close to people who will teach them, because the world may change before their parents stop working. I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 56 when robots fit doors around 2039, and I will still need pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be eighteen and twenty-three by 2036, so school expenses will not be the same, though they might still need help finding their feet. The mortgage should be lower if we keep paying, but I cannot count on a pension or on carpentry wages after 2039 robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep this job and put any extra winter overtime toward the mortgage balance rather than buying new tools on credit. Over the decade I'd take paid repair work with the lead when offered; in 2037 I'd check renovation vacancies with cousin Leena and apply only if I can show a sound repair record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy today. Ten years is a chance to pay down the house and learn from someone skilled, but it does not turn age 56 into retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say an apprenticeship with wages and someone who checks their work is worth considering. I wouldn't push either child out of school early because I did; they need choices I didn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no overtime comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we make the normal mortgage payment and keep the savings for Pavel's quiet months. I won't write extra money into the plan before it is earned.

say: I would tell the children to seek **paid teaching** before choosing work.
I would say **56** is still an age when I need wages.
think: The children’s **school bills** will change as they reach adulthood.
I cannot assume a **pension** or safe carpentry income after robots.
do: Keep **current shifts** and use actual overtime to reduce mortgage debt.
Take **paid repairs** under the lead’s checks.
Ask Leena about **renovation vacancies** in 2037 and apply if qualified.
feel: **Uneasy** about later wages, with time to reduce debt.
S4.quote: I won't write extra money into the plan before it is earned.
fieldNote: Her ten-year view includes **adult children** with different costs and no assumed pension at age 56.
She directs **earned overtime** to mortgage debt and waits for a sound repair record before changing builders.

steps.text: Keep earning paid shifts on current residential sites
Put actual winter overtime pay toward mortgage principal
Take paid supervised door-repair jobs when offered
Apply for renovation vacancies in 2037 if repair record qualifies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because the robots come by 2031 while the children are still young and the mortgage is still there. A paid adult apprenticeship and a clear answer about how many site hands the builder will keep would help. My family can cover a pickup, not a lost wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether an older beginner gets the same patience as a young apprentice. Some days I'm embarrassed to ask the lead again, but I do because a bad door stays bad after I leave. A real teacher on a paid shift would help me more than any notice about adapting.

headlineQuote: A real teacher on a paid shift would help me more than any notice about adapting.
portrait: Esther is a **43-year-old junior** residential site worker learning carpentry after leaving school early.
A **mortgage**, two school-age children and seasonal grounds wages make five months saved a necessary buffer.
She never uses **AI tools** and prefers complete, supervised physical practice.
She expects **robots** to threaten door-fitting pay and seeks a paid adult apprenticeship.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** brings robots by 2031 while her children and mortgage still require steady wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** and clear staffing figures would help her plan while family supports childcare.
